solution: For each project take prefix sums S_j of (profit - cost) over its first j floors; reaching floor j needs outside capital need_j = max over t <= j of (a_t - S_{t-1}), a running maximum, and afterwards the project has contributed S_j to the budget. A prefix is worth building purely for money only when S_j beats every earlier prefix, so keep those record prefixes as milestones. Harvest greedily with a priority queue holding each project's next milestone keyed by need_j + S_{current position} (its threshold expressed in total money, which shifts upward as the project advances because the money already includes that project's own earnings); pop and apply while the threshold is at most the current budget - the budget only grows, so this closure reaches the unique maximum capital M. Then, for every project independently, continue adding floors from the position it reached while the budget allows: such a push can never reach a new record prefix, because that record's requirement already exceeded M, so it never raises the budget above M and therefore never unlocks another project, which makes a single linear scan per project correct. Report the largest height and the smallest index attaining it; total cost O(sum of m_i * log n).
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
notes: Verified against an exhaustive brute force (BFS over the vector of built heights, since the budget is a function of that vector) on 24000 random cases with up to 4 projects and 4 floors each, plus both official samples. The subtle point that a first attempt gets wrong: a milestone's requirement need_j is measured against money EXCLUDING that project's own earnings, so a static sort of all milestones by need_j overcounts once a project has partly paid for itself - the threshold must be need_j + S_{position}, which is why a priority queue rather than one sorted sweep is the natural structure. The judge tags also list divide-and-conquer, dp and sortings; the solution above needs none of them, so they are probably alternative or heavier accepted approaches rather than the intended one, and I did not label them. Considered and rejected: exchange-argument (the greedy is justified by a monotone-closure argument, not by an adjacent swap) and binary-search-answer (nothing is being searched over).
